title: Drones strike cargo ship Chelsea 3 off Byala, Bulgaria; crew of 15 rescued
place: Black Sea, about 18 nautical miles east of Byala (Bulgarian exclusive economic zone)
summary: Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the Maltese-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was hit by three aerial drones about 18 nautical miles east of Byala, in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, during the night of 12 to 13 October 2026. All 15 crew members were rescued.
impact: The Border Police rescued all 15 crew members (seven Ukrainian and eight Azerbaijani nationals) and took them to Varna; five received treatment for minor injuries, according to BTA and BNT, while Sega reports six hurt, mostly with light burns. The ship, sailing empty from Giresun (Türkiye) to Giurgiulești (Moldova), stayed afloat and was at anchor.

The national news agency BTA and the public broadcaster BNT report the statement; Sega adds the ship's route and management. A distress signal reached Bulgaria's maritime rescue centre at about 01:30 (Sega: 01:57). Sources give the distance as 15 or 18 nautical miles off Byala.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where is not established. The exact time of the strike is not given in the cited sources.
attribution: Not established. Radev said there was no solid, clear evidence against any party, while arguing that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation; he said he would summon Russia's ambassador for talks.

title: Coalition reports incoming drones and cruise missiles over Saudi Arabia after weekend airport strikes

This followed strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on 10 and 11 October that the cited reports describe as a missile strike and an unidentified projectile, not as drone attacks.

evidence: Drones appear in this dossier only through the Saudi-led coalition's statements on Monday 12 October, as reported by Arab News and Reuters. The earlier airport strikes are not drone incidents in the cited sources: Reuters describes Saturday's deadly strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as a missile strike, and GACA said an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 on Sunday, killing a Pakistani national and injuring 11. GACA also said Dammam's King Fahd International Airport was targeted on Sunday evening, without naming the weapon. Those strikes are context only and are not attributed to drones here. Japanese broadcaster TBS, citing the Saudi-led coalition, reported that a drone hit a terminal at Riyadh's international airport on 11 October and caused a fire. That account comes from a party to the conflict and differs from GACA's statement (an unidentified projectile); it is shown as context, not as confirmation of a drone strike.
unknown: Where the reported drones were heading, how many there were, whether any were intercepted or reached a target, and who launched them are not established in the cited sources.
attribution: The cited reports do not say who launched the drones reported on Monday; they describe the alerts in the context of the Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia. The Houthis claimed Saturday's airport attack, which the cited sources do not attribute to drones.

title: Drone strikes hit Port Sudan over several days, damaging fuel depots, the airport and the main power substation
summary: From 4 May 2025 drones struck military and civilian sites in Port Sudan, the army-aligned government's wartime base on the Red Sea, over several days. Reported targets include a military base near the airport, fuel depots, the airport, a hotel near the presidential residence and the city's main power substation. Military sources blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which did not claim the attacks.
impact: Fuel depots burned, air traffic was halted on 6 May at the only airport still handling international civilian flights, and a strike on the main power substation caused a blackout across the city. The maritime security firm Ambrey reported drone strikes on the container terminal. No immediate reports of casualties were given in the AFP report. Nearly all humanitarian aid into Sudan arrives through Port Sudan, and the UN chief called the reports of attacks a worrying development.
evidence: Officials of the national electricity company and the airport confirmed drone hits, AFP and Reuters correspondents or witnesses reported explosions and smoke, and Ambrey reported drone strikes on the container terminal. Blame for the strikes rests on military sources and residents, not on a claim of responsibility or an independent investigation.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where, the type of drones, and the full extent of damage and casualties. The RSF's statement did not address the attacks. Sudan's army-aligned government accused the UAE of supplying the drones to the RSF; the UAE has consistently denied backing the RSF.
attribution: Sudanese military sources blamed the RSF, and residents told Al Jazeera they believed RSF drone strikes were responsible. The RSF did not address the attacks in a statement late on 6 May. Sudan's army-aligned government severed diplomatic relations with the UAE over alleged arming of the RSF. None of this has been independently established.

title: Drone strike damages the Chornobyl New Safe Confinement; IAEA later finds it lost its confinement function
place: Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, Kyiv region
summary: At about 01:50 on 14 February 2025 a drone struck the New Safe Confinement, the structure covering the destroyed Unit 4 reactor at the Chornobyl site, and caused a fire. The IAEA team at the site heard the explosion and saw a breach of the outer layer. In late 2025 the IAEA reported that the strike caused significant structural damage and that the structure had lost its primary safety functions, including confinement, without permanent damage to its load-bearing structures.
impact: No casualties were reported and radiation levels inside and outside the building stayed normal and stable. The IAEA later said the strike did not lead to any release of radioactive material but caused significant structural damage affecting the confinement function and projected lifetime of the structure. Limited temporary repairs were carried out on the roof, and further temporary repairs were planned for 2026 with support from the EBRD.
evidence: The IAEA team at the site heard the explosion, saw smoke, fire and the breach, and was informed by Ukraine that a drone had struck the structure. The IAEA's later statements describe the event as a drone strike, and its comprehensive safety assessment confirmed the loss of confinement capability. The IAEA did not attribute the strike.
unknown: Who launched the drone: AP reported that it was not possible to independently confirm who was behind the strike. The IAEA statements in the cited sources do not state the drone type.
attribution: Ukraine's president said a Russian drone with a high-explosive warhead hit the shell. A Kremlin spokesman denied the claim, saying Russia's military does not strike nuclear facilities. The IAEA did not attribute blame.

title: Houthi-claimed drone strikes central Tel Aviv, killing one person; Israeli military cites human error

evidence: Israeli police and emergency services reported the casualties, and the Israeli military described the drone type and its approach from Yemen. attribution: The Houthi spokesperson claimed responsibility on X and said the strike used a new drone called Yafa. Israel's military said it believed the drone arrived from Yemen. Analysts and Western intelligence services have long accused Iran of arming the Houthis, which Tehran denies.

summary: On 7 April 2024 drones struck the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the first direct targeting of the plant since November 2022 according to the IAEA. attribution: Plant officials said Ukrainian military drones carried out the attack, and Russia's IAEA ambassador accused the agency of being afraid to say Ukraine was behind it.
